title: The classical allocation of energy to the spectrum
spoken: The spectral energy density equals eight pi times the frequency squared over the speed of light cubed, times k B times the temperature.
explanation: Give every mode of the radiation the average energy k_B T that classical theory assigns, and count the modes per unit volume per unit frequency: the density grows as the frequency squared without limit.
assumptions: Each radiation mode in equilibrium carries the classical average energy k_B T.
These are modern teaching equations in SI notation; the paper writes L for c and R/N for k_B.

notes.title: Spectral energy density
notes.explanation: The same quantity section 4 describes with Wien's law, here computed from classical theory.

notes.title: Frequency
notes.explanation: Squared: the number of modes per unit frequency grows with the frequency squared, so the density does too.

notes.title: Speed of light
notes.explanation: Cubed, from counting standing waves in a box; the paper writes it L.

notes.title: Boltzmann's constant
notes.explanation: With the temperature, the classical average energy per mode; R over N in the paper.

notes.title: Temperature
notes.explanation: The density is proportional to it at every frequency in this allocation.

notes.title: No upper limit
notes.explanation: Nothing in the formula stops the growth at high frequency, so the total energy over all frequencies diverges. That is the difficulty section 1 names, before any quantum is proposed.
